description: We are six middle and high school students who combine our curiosity about space with science, storytelling, and coding. In Signal Seekers, the game we developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we tell the stories of robotic explorers on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space through interactive missions. Available in Turkish and English, our game aims to share the scientific legacy of space exploration and inspire players to experience the excitement of discovery.

details:
Some of humanity’s boldest questions are still standing on the Moon, resting on Mars, or travelling through deep space. They have wheels, mirrors, rotors, and antennas. Signal Seekers invites children to discover the stories inside those machines.

We developed Signal Seekers as a browser game for children aged 9–14, playable in Turkish and English. It brings together interactive storytelling, five mini-games, and information linked to NASA mission sources. Our response to the challenge focuses on helping children explore the scientific legacy of equipment left on the Moon and Mars. Pioneer 10 extends that journey into deep space, connecting planetary exploration with humanity’s desire to communicate beyond Earth.

A story that gives exploration a purpose

The game takes place in a fictional 2060, when memory signals from earlier space missions are fading. Players join Piko, a little star mechanic, to recover five signals and restore a cosmic memory network.

Each signal leads to a different mission. As players progress, they discover what an explorer investigated, how it worked, and why its contribution matters. Recovering memories is our storytelling metaphor for keeping scientific knowledge alive. The missions use simplified, symbolic gameplay inspired by real exploration.

Five missions, five ways to participate

The Laser Bridge: Players aim a laser at a lunar reflector and complete successful reflections. The activity introduces the idea behind measuring the Earth–Moon distance with light.

Traces of Water: Players guide Opportunity across the Martian landscape, collecting hematite clues while avoiding rocks. The mission connects exploration with the search for evidence of past water.

The Impossible Flight: Players control Ingenuity’s altitude and pass through signal rings. Its story introduces the challenge of powered flight in the thin Martian atmosphere.

The Heart of Mars: Players observe and repeat vibration sequences associated with InSight. The activity introduces seismic investigation and the planet’s crust, mantle, and core.

A Letter to the Stars: Players navigate Pioneer 10 through an asteroid field and collect pieces of its message plaque. The mission connects space exploration with the human wish to share who we are and where we come from.

Turning progress into discovery

Completing a mini-game opens an imaginative radio diary written from the explorer’s perspective. Players then encounter a fact card linked to a NASA source and answer a science question.

This sequence connects action with explanation. Players collect Science Sparks and unlock entries in the Cosmic Museum, where they can revisit the scientific legacy of different missions. Completing all five missions unlocks a personalized Memory Guardian Certificate.

The explorers’ voices are fictional. The interface clearly distinguishes these creative passages from the scientific information in the fact cards.

How we built it

We developed the game using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. HTML provides the page structure, CSS shapes the visual presentation and responsive layout, and JavaScript manages the missions, controls, language switching, questions, and progress.

HTML Canvas supports the animated game scenes. Browser audio provides synthesized sound effects, while localStorage saves progress in the player’s browser. The project runs through a public GitHub Pages link, allowing visitors to access it without creating an account or installing software.

Our scientific reference material comes from NASA mission pages and NASA’s lunar laser-ranging information. We use these sources to explain the missions and provide direct links for further exploration.

The choices behind the experience

We designed each mini-game around the scientific purpose of its mission. A reflector returns light, a rover searches for clues, a helicopter navigates the sky, and a seismic instrument detects patterns. These connections give the player’s actions meaning within the story.

We also considered language, age, controls, and the experience of making mistakes. Turkish and English options allow players to explore in either language. Keyboard, mouse, and touch controls support different devices. Sound controls and a reduced-motion option provide additional choices. Missed rings, incorrect sequences, and collisions allow players to continue trying.

The tone is hopeful and curious. The explorers speak with warmth and personality, helping children approach unfamiliar scientific ideas through characters they can remember.

The impact we aim to create

We want children to connect spacecraft names with the questions those missions helped humanity investigate. We aim to encourage curiosity about evidence, introduce reliable scientific sources, and invite players to ask questions of their own.

Our project’s creative contribution lies in bringing mission-inspired gameplay, fictional first-person storytelling, and sourced scientific information into one continuous journey. Each recovered signal carries a discovery forward to a new audience.

The story ends by passing that curiosity to the player:

They opened the way. The next discovery could be yours.

Play Signal Seekers:

https://sbnmkyl.github.io/signal-seekers-space-game/
